Transform Outcome to Linear Predictor

Source: R/YtoLP.R
Y_to_LP.Rd

Uses the Julia function 'Y_to_LP' to convert observed responses to linear predictors using canonical link functions from generalized linear models (GLMs).

Usage

Y_to_LP(
  Y,
  family,
  shape = NULL,
  n_trials = NULL,
  std = NULL,
  theta = NULL,
  n_categories = NULL
)

Arguments

Y

A numeric vector or matrix of observed responses.

family

A character string indicating the GLM family to use.

shape

Optional shape parameter (accepted for consistency; unused).

n_trials

Optional number of trials (used for the Binomial family).

std

Optional standard deviation (accepted for consistency; unused).

theta

Optional NegativeBinomial size (accepted for consistency; unused).

n_categories

Optional number of categories for "Multinomial" (default: the largest observed category).

Value

A numeric vector or matrix representing the linear predictor.

Details

Applies the family's link function to the observed responses, with a small adjustment so the link is finite at the boundary: logit with 0 and 1 replaced by 0.01 and 0.99 (Bernoulli, Binomial), and \(\log(Y + 0.1)\) for the log-link families. The families match LP_to_Y():

FamilyLinkExtra arguments
"Normal"identitystd (default 1)
"Bernoulli"logit
"Binomial"logitn_trials (required)
"Poisson"log
"Gamma"log (mean \(e^\eta\))shape (default 1)
"Exponential"log
"InverseGaussian"logshape (\(\lambda\), default 1)
"NegativeBinomial"logtheta (size, default 1)
"Geometric"log
"MultivariateNormal"identitycov_matrix (required)
"Multinomial"baseline-category logitn_categories (required)
"Cox"null-model deviance residuals

For "Cox", Y is an \(n \times 2\) matrix with columns time and status (1 = event, 0 = censored), as returned by LP_to_Y(family = "Cox"), or a survival::Surv() object. The result is the deviance residual of the null Cox model (Therneau, Grambsch and Fleming, 1990): with the Nelson-Aalen cumulative hazard \(\hat\Lambda_0\), the martingale residual \(M_i = \delta_i - \hat\Lambda_0(t_i)\) is made more symmetric as \(D_i = \mathrm{sign}(M_i)\sqrt{-2[M_i + \delta_i \log(\delta_i - M_i)]}\). It increases with the linear predictor and is meant for variable selection; fit the selected model with survival::coxph().

For "Multinomial", Y holds categories \(1, \dots, K\) and the result is an \(n \times (K-1)\) matrix of baseline-category logits of the smoothed one-hot vector \((\mathrm{onehot}(Y_i) + 0.01)/(1 + 0.01K)\). For "Binomial", the logit is multiplied by n_trials. GLM stands for generalized linear model, a common framework for regression models.

The underlying Julia logic is sourced from 'Y_to_LP.jl', and relies on the 'JuliaCall' interface.

References

Therneau, T. M., Grambsch, P. M. and Fleming, T. R. (1990). Martingale-based residuals for survival models. Biometrika, 77(1), 147–160. doi:10.1093/biomet/77.1.147

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
if (interactive() && requireNamespace("JuliaCall", quietly = TRUE)) {
  julia_ready <- FALSE
  tryCatch({
    JuliaCall::julia_setup(installJulia = FALSE)
    julia_ready <- TRUE
  }, error = function(e) message("Julia setup failed"))

  if (julia_ready) {
    Y1 <- rbinom(100, 1, 0.5)
    eta1 <- Y_to_LP(Y1, family = "Bernoulli")

    Y2 <- rpois(100, lambda = 5)
    eta2 <- Y_to_LP(Y2, family = "Poisson")

    print(head(eta1))
    print(head(eta2))
  }
}
} # }
